key_messages: Scattered showers, with steadier rain primarily in southern and eastern Vermont, will persist through this evening as a Nor'easter departs to the northeast. A slow clearing trend will occur tomorrow with dry weather returning.
High pressure will keep our region dry over the next few days along with a warming trend and variable cloudiness. Localized breezy conditions will develop on Thursday.
Several rounds of showers possible late week and this weekend.

National Weather Service Burlington VT
239 PM EDT Mon Sep 28 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 239 PM EDT Monday...

No substantial changes were made.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 239 PM EDT Monday...

1. Scattered showers, with steadier rain primarily in southern 
and eastern Vermont, will persist through this evening as a 
Nor'easter departs to the northeast. A slow clearing trend will 
occur tomorrow with dry weather returning.

2. High pressure will keep our region dry over the next few 
days along with a warming trend and variable cloudiness. Localized 
breezy conditions will develop on Thursday.

3. Several rounds of showers possible late week and this 
weekend.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 239 PM EDT Monday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: A very well defined low pressure center spinning 
northeastward continues to be evident on satellite imagery and will 
approach Cape Cod this evening. The system's upper level low is 
displaced well to the northwest over southern New England, and most 
of the rain is located on its northwestern flank with observed 
rainfall rates near 0.1"/hour. As the upper low tracks farther north 
early this evening, bands of light to moderate rain will slide that 
way such that steadier rain should move across all of central and 
eastern Vermont before exiting to our east tonight. Additional 
rainfall in this swath is likely to be in the range of 0.1" to 0.5", 
which will lead to storm totals localized in southern Windsor County 
approaching 2", but with most of the region in the 0.25" to 1" 
range. 

As rain comes to an end, there will still be a lot of low level 
moisture and only modest drying aloft from the north-northwest 
overnight. Hence, expect early morning low clouds with the 925-850 
millibar layer remaining saturated, and perhaps localized fog almost 
areawide with perhaps exceptions in the lee of some of the higher 
peaks such as near Schroon Lake, NY. As the day progresses, cyclonic 
flow will linger and help maintain a thin layer of shallow clouds 
such that mountains remain obscured, slowly improving from west to 
east as top-down drying occurs. Only as the weakening upper level 
low departs into southern Maine or Gulf of Maine, much of western 
portions of northern New York will trend sunny while clearing 
remains limited to late in the day in much of Vermont. The cloud 
cover will lead to only a small variation in temperature from 
sunrise to sunset again as in recent days. Areas that see a longer 
period of sunshine such as in the St. Lawrence Valley should be 
several degrees warmer, where highs will approach 70 degrees.

KEY MESSAGE 2: The main forecasting challenge mid-week will be 
related to low clouds and fog, particularly Wednesday morning. 
The air mass looks a little too warm to be dealing with frost 
potential, with above normal 850 millibar temperatures near 50 
degrees requiring an extremely strong subsidence. We will have 
seasonably moist air still in place following the early week 
rain and humid conditions, and boundary layer winds will be 
quite light as deep layer ridging moves overhead. This is a 
near-ideal setup for temperatures to drop well below crossover 
values. And as a result, widespread patchy and dense valley fog 
is likely, especially given how long our nights are this time of
year.

Aside from some higher altitude clouds, a tranquil period
Wednesday into Thursday is expected as temperatures verge on
unseasonably warm. Based on the latest blend of models, high
temperatures in the lower elevations across Vermont and the 
Champlain Valley on Thursday will likely be in the 75 to 80 
range. This would put the daily record high at Montpelier in
some jeopardy (about a 20% chance of at least tying the current
record from 2002). One other notable aspect on Thursday will be
modest southerly/southwesterly channeled flow. Have boosted
winds on Lake Champlain, with soundings showing favorable
conditions especially in the morning hours when sustained winds
could be above 20 knots. Likewise, have increased wind gusts in
the wide valleys with potential for 30+ mph values. An
approaching cold front and the increased flow out in front of
this system later in the day points to seasonably stronger 
winds in the St. Lawrence Valley, approaching 40 MPH in a 
reasonable higher end scenario. Given climatology, sustained
winds look marginally strong in this area but gusts will not be
impactful.

KEY MESSAGE 3: A weak cold front looks poised to bring scattered 
showers to the region late Friday afternoon and Friday night. The 
lack of thermal gradient on the back side of the cold front will 
limit overall vertical ascent which will likely bring just a round 
of light rain to the region. High pressure will build into the 
region Saturday morning with clearing skies expected through the day 
with light winds. Another round of rainfall looks possible on Sunday 
as a low pressure system moves off the Virginia coastline and up the 
east coast. This system will be significantly more transient that 
this past Nor'easter which makes the window of rainfall much 
smaller. There remains a lot of uncertainty regarding the track of 
this low pressure system but the trends have been further south and 
east. Some correction in low track is expected over the next few 
days but Sunday could be on the wet side if the low tracks further 
inland over the weekend. Thereafter, high pressure will build back 
into the region for early next week with seasonally cool 
temperatures expected.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z MONDAY THROUGH SATURDAY/...
Through 18Z Tuesday...Widespread MVFR to localized IFR ceilings
continue this afternoon as a Nor'Easter remains off the east 
coast. We should see a gradual decrease in ceiling height by 21Z
as flow becomes more northerly with a sharper decrease in 
ceilings after 00Z. The idea is that most places drop to 200 to 
600 ft overnight with only gradual improvement back to MVFR 
conditions expected by 16Z on Tuesday. Winds will remain light 
out of the north during this timeframe. Scattered showers this 
afternoon may bring a brief reduction in visibility but no 
significant obscurations are anticipated at this time.

Outlook...

Tuesday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Wednesday: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Wednesday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Thursday: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Thursday Night: Mainly VFR, with local MVFR possible. Chance
SHRA.
Friday: Mainly VFR, with areas MVFR possible. Chance SHRA.
Friday Night: Mainly VFR, with local MVFR possible. NO SIG WX.
Saturday: VFR. NO SIG WX.

&&
